channel.title: Deseret News - Faith
channel.description: Faith news and stories from Deseret News

item.title: Latter-day Saints among the most likely Americans to report happy family life, says major new study
item.description: A Pew Research Center survey released Tuesday found that Hindus, Jewish people and Latter-day Saints are the American religious groups most likely to describe their family lives as excellent or very good, with close to 70% of Latter-day Saints rating theirs positively. Pew drew on a larger study conducted between July 2023 and March 2024, interviewing 565 self-identified Latter-day Saints and 316 former members, with a margin of error of 6.2%. The findings portray Latter-day Saints as among the most religious adults in the country, praying and attending services more often than any other group, while also showing greater internal diversity and weaker retention. Pew noted that the softer religiosity and retention figures generally track broader national movement toward secularization. The survey covered only the United States, even though most church members live elsewhere, and it lands as the church reports record convert baptisms and missionary numbers.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Sister Yee invites Utah Valley Institute students to be the Lord’s hands in caring for those in need
item.description: Sister Kristin M. Yee, second counselor in the Relief Society general presidency, addressed a full chapel and overflow of students at the Utah Valley Institute of Religion in Orem. She told the audience they were meant to change the world through Jesus Christ and said no greater cause exists for them to take up. Yee tied that capacity to their baptismal and temple covenants and to exercising priesthood authority in their callings and assignments. The Deseret News item is a brief summary that points readers to TheChurchNews.com for the full account.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ opposes abortion measure in a second state
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has come out against a Nevada abortion ballot initiative, marking the second state where it has taken such a position, according to a letter the Deseret News authenticated. The letter went to the church's 339 Nevada congregations and was signed by General Authority Seventies Michael A. Dunn, Joaquin E. Costa and Pedro X. Larreal of the U.S. Southwest Area Presidency, who instructed local leaders to read it from the pulpit on the last two Sundays of September. A separate area presidency letter asked members in Idaho to oppose a comparable measure there. At issue in Nevada is Question 6, the Right to Abortion initiative on the Nov. 3 ballot, which would write a right to abortion into the state constitution; it already passed in 2024 with 64% of the vote and must clear a second consecutive even-year election under state law. The Nevada Catholic Conference and Catholic bishops are also campaigning against it.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Jimmer Fredette, Steve Young, 6 apostles to speak at Latter-day Saint college devotionals
item.description: An excerpt from the weekly ChurchBeat newsletter lays out the fall devotional speaker lineup at the five colleges and universities sponsored by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Steve Young, a member of both the Pro Football and College Football halls of fame, speaks at BYU-Idaho on Nov. 17, and Jimmer Fredette, who played for Team USA's 3x3 basketball team at the 2024 Olympics, speaks Nov. 10 at BYU-Hawaii. At least one apostle is scheduled at each of the five schools, with six appearing across the season. BYU-Hawaii President John “Keoni” Kauwe said this week the church has roughly 3 million college-age members, and the church heavily subsidizes tuition for the 150,000 students at its schools. It also runs a global Institute program serving 350,000 students at 2,700 locations tied to other colleges.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Kansas’ first Latter-day Saint temple opens for tours. Here are photos
item.description: Media tours of the Wichita Kansas Temple began Monday, marking the first open house for a Latter-day Saint temple in Kansas. Public tours run from Thursday, Sept. 24, through Oct. 10, free and open to all ages and faiths, with closures on Sundays and on Saturday, Oct. 3, for the church's semiannual general conference. Elder Patrick Kearon of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles will dedicate the temple on Sunday, Nov. 1. President Russell M. Nelson announced the Wichita temple in April 2022 general conference and construction started in September 2024; it will serve roughly 40,000 Latter-day Saints statewide, including more than 14,500 in the immediate region, who previously traveled to Oklahoma or Missouri. A church news release says the design draws on the area's wheat fields and sunflowers, with an interior palette of sage green, golden wheat, soft paprika and buttercream.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: A bright future for American faith? Reasons for optimism in Latter-day Saint data
item.description: The Deseret News examines why American religious decline and religious deepening appear to be happening at once, using Latter-day Saint data as a case study. The piece opens with President Dallin H. Oaks' 23-minute address at the Washington National Cathedral on the U.S. Constitution as a vehicle for peacemaking, religious freedom and unity, and the panel afterward in which Rabbi David Saperstein noted that worship attendance, belief in God and religiously grounded identity remain strong even as affiliation falls. BYU professor Justin Dyer told the paper that people less inclined toward religion now shed their religious identity more readily than in the past. The article then aggregates 10 patterns from the past decade, beginning with Church News reporting by Dave Schneider showing membership rose in 49 of 50 states over 25 years, led in percentage terms by North Dakota, Tennessee, Arkansas, Texas and North Carolina, plus the District of Columbia. California was the lone state to shrink, though it still ranks second in members behind Utah.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Hess

item.title: Church celebrates 40 years in Democratic Republic of the Congo
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is marking 40 years in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which granted the faith legal recognition in 1986 when the country was still known as Zaire. Membership has grown from a small group to about 160,000, supported by seven missions, a missionary training center, one dedicated temple and three additional temples under construction or in planning. A commemorative ceremony held in Kinshasa on Sept. 3 drew government officials, religious leaders, church leaders and members from across the country. The Africa Newsroom reported that the event also honored Congolese pioneers whose perseverance helped establish the church there.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Kalani Sitake’s course changed because President Dallin H. Oaks gave this charge to LaVell Edwards
item.description: In an excerpt from the weekly ChurchBeat newsletter, Tad Walch traces how an assignment Dallin H. Oaks handed LaVell Edwards as BYU's president — to overturn the assumption that returned missionaries could not play productive football — eventually reshaped Kalani Sitake's life. BYU had exactly one returned missionary on the roster when Edwards took up the charge. In 1994, seven games into the season and just after the freshman fullback then listed as Kalani Fifita helped beat Notre Dame 21-14 in South Bend, older teammates Jack Damuni and Stan and John Raass told the rookie to hold Edwards on the sideline so they could dump Gatorade on him. Summoned to the coach's office that Monday and braced for a reprimand, Sitake instead heard Edwards say he would make a fine missionary and wished he had served one himself; Sitake entered the Missionary Training Center that January. Now in his 11th season as head coach with 64 returned missionaries on his roster, Sitake recalled at a spring alumni event the voicemail Edwards left during a rough 1-3 start in 2016 telling him to worry about the players rather than the record.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Women fuel new record as Church of Jesus Christ reaches 90,000 missionaries
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced Friday that its missionary force has topped 90,000 for the first time, surpassing the 88,500 mark set in July and far above the 78,596 counted in 2025 — a 14.5% jump. Sister missionaries now exceed 30,000, the most ever, and the surge follows a November change dropping the minimum age for women from 19 to 18, with the effect delayed until spring high school graduations; the largest contingent comes from the United States. Fifty-five missions opened worldwide in July, spread across Africa, the U.S., South America, the Philippines, the Pacific, Europe, Canada, Asia and Mexico, and the additional 11,000-plus missionaries have filled them, bringing the global total to 506. The growth coincides with more than 900,000 converts over three years, including 385,490 baptisms in 2025, and with record seminary and institute enrollment of 1.09 million. Church President Dallin H. Oaks, who signaled the coming records to new mission leaders in June, attributes the trend to a message about Jesus Christ that he says leaves people happier and better equipped for life's difficulties; a demographic bulge of 18-year-olds is also a factor, one expected to be followed by a national decline in that age group.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: More internet is associated with less faith, according to a new analysis of 81 countries
item.description: Sociologists at Slovenia's University of Maribor report in a new paper, "Internet Diffusion and Religious Decline: Evidence from 81 Countries, 1990-2022," that rising internet penetration within a country tracks with falling religiosity on a six-item composite drawn from World Values Survey data. The effect concentrates in institutional belonging and whether people call themselves religious, while links to attendance at services and trust in churches are weaker and frequently not significant. The authors controlled for education, income, urbanization, globalization, immigration and population aging, and say the pattern is not merely a side effect of growing wealth or schooling, though they concede their correlational design cannot establish causation and that the survey was administered unevenly across countries and years. Deseret News writer Jacob Hess situates the study alongside a University of Michigan finding that 42 of the same countries turned sharply less religious between 2007 and 2020 after 49 had been gaining religious commitment up to 2007, and an earlier estimate crediting the internet with as much as a fifth of the drop in U.S. religious affiliation from the 1980s to 2010. BYU scholar Barbara Morgan Gardner has similarly linked heavy social media use to faith transitions while emphasizing the wider secular culture that Notre Dame's Christian Smith describes, though the Maribor authors caution that the decline is neither uniform across nations nor across traditions.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Hess

item.title: Latter-day Saint leaders join other faiths to oppose Idaho abortion vote
item.description: Leaders of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints have come out against the Idaho Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act, a Nov. 3 ballot initiative that would create a state right to abortion. A letter sent to the faith's 1,300 Idaho congregations, to be read from the pulpit over the next two Sundays, asks members to voice their opposition respectfully and with what it calls Christlike love and civility in political discourse, and says the church is joining like-minded individuals and organizations. The letter carries the signatures of the U.S. Central Area Presidency: Elders José A. Teixeira, Ricardo P. Giménez, Karl Hirst and James Fantone. The measure would follow 11 states that have established abortion rights since the U.S. Supreme Court found no federal right four years ago, according to Ballotpedia. Roman Catholics in Idaho mobilized earlier, with Boise Bishop Peter F. Christensen writing in July that the initiative is radically pro-abortion and would dismantle existing protections, prompting months of pro-life masses and Friday prayer and fasting.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ expands tools for musical worship
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has added music features to its Gospel Library app aimed at helping members bring sacred music into everyday worship and gospel study, according to a release on ChurchofJesusChrist.org. The centerpiece is a playlist function reachable from the home screen icon, where users scroll to a Playlists section offering curated collections with names such as Hymns Reimagined and Acoustic Hymns. Sliding right reveals options to browse all playlists or build a personal one, and users can mix in hymns, general conference talks, scripture chapters and other Gospel Library material that has audio. The church framed the tools as a response to leaders' calls for fuller participation in worship, citing Elder Patrick Kearon of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, who urged in a recent video that congregational singing be transformed with an energetic tempo and remembrance of Jesus Christ.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: What the Constitution requires of us, according to President Oaks at the National Cathedral
item.description: President Dallin H. Oaks of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints told a capacity audience of 4,000 at the National Cathedral in Washington on Wednesday that sharing a country does not require Americans to agree, and that working alongside people you disagree with is exactly what the Constitution demands. Delivering the address on the eve of Constitution Day as the nation marks 250 years since its founding, he said the document compels a divided people to form coalitions and act together for the common good, calling it a model for a diverse people to achieve self-government. The speech was part of the cathedral's 'A Better Way' series, which convenes bipartisan leaders to encourage civil discourse and mutual understanding. Oaks, a constitutional scholar and former Utah Supreme Court justice, has long argued for listening to opposing views and balancing competing rights in a pluralistic democracy. In a 2021 address at the University of Virginia he made a similar case for resolving differences through mutual respect, shared understanding and good-faith negotiation.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: Behind the scenes of general conference: ‘Audio and Light’
item.description: A Church News piece profiles the technical crews who ready the Conference Center's sound and lighting systems ahead of general conference. Their pre-event checks cover the venue's fixtures, speakers, microphones and visual elements, with the goal of keeping the broadcast free of distractions for viewers and those in the hall. Broadcast and events producer Jody Hadfield likened the operation to a ship's crew, where the result depends on many specialists each executing a well-understood role.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Understand needs, forge solutions, President Oaks invites at Washington National Cathedral
item.description: President Dallin H. Oaks spoke at the Washington National Cathedral on Wednesday, Sept. 16, on the eve of Constitution Day, calling for common ground in preserving religious freedom after seven decades studying the U.S. Constitution. He opened by saying he speaks for no political party or pressure group but for the Constitution itself, which he called a model for a diverse people to achieve self-government. Oaks was sustained as president of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in October 2025 and has served as an apostle for 42 years; he previously clerked for U.S. Supreme Court Chief Justice Earl Warren, taught law for 15 years, and sat on the Utah Supreme Court for more than three years before his 1984 call to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. He recounted the expulsion of early church members from Missouri in the 1830s and their migration west beyond U.S. borders in the 1840s, describing those pioneers as refugees. Those experiences, he said, taught early members what it meant to become peacemakers.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Jensen

item.title: When faith becomes a custody battle
item.description: A Maine custody dispute between Emily Bickford and Matthew Bradeen illustrates how religious upbringing can become the center of a legal fight between separated parents. The two agreed roughly a decade ago to share parental rights over their now 13-year-old daughter, making decisions about education and medical care jointly whenever possible. That arrangement frayed in 2021 after Bickford began taking the girl to Calvary Chapel Greater Portland without Bradeen's consent, and he later learned she was to be baptized. Court documents say the church's verse-by-verse Bible teaching included vivid descriptions of Hell that left the child frightened and anxious, and allege that messages she received there alienated her from her father, while the pastor addressed the legal case and prayed at length about it during a service. The parents brought in experts on cults during mediation as they tried to resolve the disagreement.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: Apostle asks BYU students to ‘settle in their hearts’ their faith in 10 essential truths
item.description: Elder Neil L. Andersen of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles told 14,898 people at BYU's weekly Marriott Center devotional Tuesday that students should work to get their faith in Jesus Christ and devotion to the restored gospel settled in their hearts. He described that settling as having spiritually weighed the blessings and sacrifices of discipleship and then choosing, through agency, to commit to that path without continuing to doubt the decision. Andersen said he reached that point himself as a BYU student in 1973, and observed that students today face an overload of information and misinformation at the dawn of the AI age. He joked that if Robert Frost were writing 'The Road Not Taken' now, the poem might open with one hundred roads diverging in a yellow wood. Quoting Luke 14 from Joseph Smith's translation of the Bible, the former business leader said making faith in the Savior central to one's motivations and decisions requires unusual clarity of purpose, humility and firmness of mind.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Episode 312: First couple sealed in San Diego temple reflects 3 decades later
item.description: Elizabeth and Giovanni Guanuna, who in April 1993 became the first couple sealed in the San Diego California Temple after its original dedication, are the guests on episode 312 of the Church News podcast. Reporter Aimee Cobabe interviewed them on the temple grounds during its August 2026 rededication weekend, roughly three decades after their marriage there. The conversation covers the significance they attach to that sealing and the role temple service has played in their faith since.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ advances 3 temples across the U.S. and South America
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced in a press release Monday that three temples are advancing toward completion — two in the United States and one in South America. The Colorado Springs Colorado Temple broke ground Saturday, Sept. 12, while construction on the Cincinnati Ohio and La Paz Bolivia temples is set to begin in November. Elder Karl D. Hirst of the church's United States Central Area Presidency presided over the Colorado Springs groundbreaking and dedicated the site, calling temples places of spiritual guidance, peace, hope and revelation and literally the house of the Lord. The Colorado Springs temple was announced in October 2023 and is planned as a single-story building of about 45,000 square feet. The Cincinnati and La Paz temples were announced in 2024 and 2021, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Utah Catholic Conference to gather Catholics from across Utah
item.description: The Catholic Diocese of Salt Lake City will hold its third annual Utah Catholic Conference on Saturday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. at the Skaggs Catholic Center in Draper, drawing Catholics from across the state. Bishop Oscar A. Solis will preside, calling the gathering a special chance for the diocese to come together as one church to learn, grow, pray and strengthen their faith. Crystal Painter, director of the diocese's Marriage and Family Life Office, said she was very excited for this year's event, themed 'Sacred Heart, Heart of the Mission.' The conference began as a training session limited to diocesan leaders before Solis opened it to the public three years ago, and Painter said it has grown each year as an expression of the bishop's emphasis on comprehensive faith formation for people at every stage of life. Attendees are directed to park at Juan Diego Catholic High School in Draper.
item.dc:creator: Joe Wirthlin

item.title: Latter-day Saint apostle explores patterns for finding direction in a ‘messed up’ world
item.description: Elder David A. Bednar of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles turned the BYU Marriott Center into what he called the largest classroom in the history of the world on Sunday, leading a discussion rather than delivering a sermon to more than 18,000 young single adults from the church's Utah Area. He was joined on stage by his wife, other church leaders and a panel of young single adults for a conversation about searching the scriptures for patterns and personal direction. Bednar said the scriptures contain endless patterns useful to lifelong disciples of Jesus Christ, and that powerful patterns can be drawn from seemingly ordinary as well as unusual scriptural events. He described the scriptures as the prerecorded voice of the Lord, through which the Holy Ghost delivers messages each person needs individually. His invitation to listeners was to discern the personal messages the Spirit communicates to them through that study.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Dedication date announced for third Latter-day Saint temple in Tennessee
item.description: The First Presidency of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced that the Knoxville Tennessee Temple will be dedicated Sunday, March 7, 2027, by Elder David A. Bednar of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. A free public open house for guests of all faiths and ages will run Monday through Saturday from Jan. 27 through Feb. 13, preceded by media tours on Jan. 25 and private tours for invited guests on Jan. 26. The temple was first announced in April 2022 by the late church President Russell M. Nelson, with construction beginning in January 2024. Once dedicated it will be the third operating temple in Tennessee, joining those in Memphis and Nashville. Together the three will serve roughly 62,000 Latter-day Saints in the state.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Dedication, open house dates announced for Smithfield Utah Temple
item.description: The First Presidency announced in a press release Monday that the Smithfield Utah Temple will be dedicated Sunday, April 18, 2027, by Elder Quentin L. Cook of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, following a free public open house. The dedication falls just over six months after the Ephraim Utah Temple is dedicated on Oct. 11, and closely follows the April 1 start of the Salt Lake Temple's six-month open house. Plans for the three-story Smithfield temple were announced by then-President Russell M. Nelson at April 2021 general conference, and construction began in June 2022. Utah, home to more than 2.2 million Latter-day Saints, currently counts 32 announced temples. Church President Dallin H. Oaks recently taught that the temple is essential to the church's doctrine on the family because its ordinances allow families to return together to the presence of God.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: 3 first cousins serve as bishops in neighboring Othello, Washington, wards
item.description: Three of the bishops leading neighboring wards in the Othello Washington Stake, in a farming city in central Washington, are first cousins to one another. Scott J. Harris took over the Othello 3rd Ward in 2022, David K. Beus the 1st Ward in 2023 and E. Brian Gentry the 2nd Ward in 2024, with all three descending from local farming pioneers Evan and Alta Beus through parents who are siblings. The men suspect their differing surnames kept the stake president from realizing the family connection when he extended the callings.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: How faith in God sustained a U.S. airman shot down over Iran
item.description: A U.S. Air Force weapons systems officer identified by the call sign Bravo told CBS News that faith sustained him through 50 hours on the ground in Iran after his F-15E was shot down. On April 3, five weeks into the war, Bravo and his pilot, call sign Alpha, launched a nighttime strike on Iranian facilities when an Iranian missile struck their aircraft with what he described as the force of a freight train, forcing both men to eject over the heart of Iran. Bravo's parachute had been damaged in the hit, and he recalled looking up to see no canopy as the most terrifying moment of his life, prompting him to pray that God's will be done but that he needed help. Military briefers estimate he hit the ground at 70 to 100 miles per hour. He then spent more than two days evading Iranian bounty hunters, coping with severe injuries and trying to reach U.S. forces before rescue came at sunrise on Easter morning.
item.dc:creator: Emily Walker

item.title: Children learn about families in September Friend to Friend with Elder Caussé, Primary general presidency
item.description: Elder Gérald Caussé of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and his wife, Sister Valérie Caussé, were featured guests on the September 2026 "Friend to Friend" broadcast from The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, released Sunday, Sept. 13. During the segment, the couple made crêpes alongside child hosts Leki Uipi and Millie Ferreira while sharing family traditions tied to the church's "Family Proclamation." Elder Caussé testified that family is central to God's plan and that eternal happiness comes through living as families who support and love one another. The broadcast is aimed at teaching children about the importance of family through relatable, hands-on storytelling.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Opinion: I walked around the Salt Lake Temple again. It was worth the wait
item.description: In a Deseret News opinion piece, writer Samuel Hislop describes walking the newly opened grounds of the Salt Lake Temple for the first time in nearly seven years, as construction fencing has come down ahead of the 2027 open house. Hislop reflects on touching the temple's quartz monzonite stone and bronze door handles, comparing the communal act of circling a sacred building to the Islamic Tawaf around the Kaaba, and draws on scholars' commentary that early Christians understood "temple" as a description of a gathered community rather than only a building. He frames the nearly seven-year renovation, delayed in part by the pandemic, through the biblical symbolism of the number seven as completion, comparing the wait to the ancient Israelites' exile from Jerusalem. The piece closes by casting the coming year before the temple's six-month 2027 celebration as a kind of sabbath season of rest and gratitude after years of construction.
item.dc:creator: Samuel Hislop

item.title: Sister Yee sees great faith in Europe Central Area ministry assignment
item.description: Sister Kristin M. Yee, second counselor in the Relief Society general presidency of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, ministered across Germany, Austria, Cyprus and Spain during a Europe Central Area assignment from Aug. 28 through Sept. 7. Her stops included instruction for local Relief Society, Young Women and Primary leaders, along with devotionals for missionaries, temple workers and young adults, according to the church's Europe Newsroom. Yee said she expects to remember the "beautiful faces of great faith" she encountered more than the countries she visited. The item points readers to TheChurchNews.com for the full report.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Meet the college students hungry for something more exciting than culture war
item.description: Student leaders from 24 college campuses gathered in August at BYU's Peacemaker Project-hosted National Student Conference for Peacemaking, pushing back on the narrative that campus life is defined by contentious division. Organizers Alex and Mirabella Keogh said the effort grew out of Church President Russell M. Nelson's 2023 “Peacemakers Needed” address and said students they've met across dozens of universities are eager for spaces to disagree respectfully rather than treat opponents as enemies. BridgeUSA's Ross Irwin said students increasingly tell him politics have damaged their own families and that they're searching for places to voice honest opinions without being shut out. A Baylor student who attended said she returned from Utah more hopeful about the country despite its polarization.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Hess, Deseret News

item.title: 5 Latter-day Saints reflect on Sept. 11 experiences that shaped their faith
item.description: As the nation marked the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, Church History Department oral histories captured Latter-day Saints' memories of that day, including Kristopher Woolley, then a 27-year-old Goldman Sachs analyst who watched the second plane strike the World Trade Center's south tower from his 50th-floor office and was walking toward the towers to help when the south tower collapsed nearby. Woolley described the moment the clear morning turned to what felt like a volcanic eruption of ash and debris. The broader collection, recorded by the church's Church History Department, gathers accounts from five members whose experiences that day shaped their faith, part of the church's ongoing effort to preserve firsthand memories of the attacks.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: On eve of Constitution Day, President Oaks will speak at the Washington National Cathedral
item.description: Church President Dallin H. Oaks, a former Utah Supreme Court justice and University of Chicago law professor, will address the nation from Washington National Cathedral on Sept. 16, the eve of Constitution Day, as part of an event called “Faith, Freedom and the Common Good” focused on religious liberty and the Constitution. The Deseret News compiled five representative quotes from Oaks' decades of teaching on the topic, including his argument that religious values remain interlinked with sustaining constitutional freedoms, that Latter-day Saints have a unique responsibility to defend constitutional principles, and that conflicting claims over rights are best resolved through mutual understanding rather than fear. Oaks has spoken on these themes throughout his roughly 42 years as a church leader.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz, Deseret News

item.title: How a filmmaker couple learned to tell stories about suffering
item.description: Filmmakers Josh Sabey and Sarah Perkins, who moved with their children to rural Arbon, Idaho after a wrongful child-abuse investigation temporarily separated them from their two sons, have built a career making documentaries that seek common ground on divisive topics like Columbine, abortion and mental health rather than partisan arguments. Perkins, who studied the biblical story of Job's suffering in her academic work, said their own ordeal echoed that narrative once their children were removed from their Massachusetts home over a since-cleared abuse allegation. Their latest project examines the contentious rebuilding of the World Trade Center site after 9/11, for which they interviewed dozens of stakeholders in Brooklyn; Sabey said he was struck that interview subjects cried more over today's political estrangement between friends and family than over 9/11 itself. The couple sees storytelling itself as an act of insisting suffering and division matter enough to be understood and remembered.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos, Deseret News

item.title: An Idaho pioneer town welcomes public to new Montpelier temple
item.description: Montpelier, Idaho, a town of fewer than 3,000 residents settled along the Oregon Trail more than 160 years ago, held a Sept. 8 media day for its new Latter-day Saint temple ahead of an Oct. 18, 2026 dedication. Elder Mark D. Eddy, a General Authority Seventy and assistant executive director of the Church's Temple Department, said the building honors the area's pioneer heritage and will serve about 15,000 local members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The report was published by Church News, a Deseret-affiliated publication, which pointed readers to TheChurchNews.com for its full coverage.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: President Uchtdorf salutes training missionaries for ‘Here am I, send me’ willingness
item.description: President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, acting president of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, addressed missionaries at an evening devotional at the Provo Missionary Training Center on Tuesday, Sept. 8, alongside his wife, Sister Harriet Uchtdorf. According to Church News, Uchtdorf praised the missionaries for choosing to serve, quoting Isaiah 6:8's declaration "Here am I; send me" as an example of exercising agency. He also paraphrased a line from the "Harry Potter" book series, telling missionaries that "it is your choices, not just your abilities, which show who you truly are." The devotional also touched on themes of invitations, goal-setting, faith and enduring in service without growing weary, per Church News' report.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Conspiracy thinking can undermine faith | Opinion
item.description: In a Deseret News opinion piece, faith and perspective writer Jacob Hess examines how immersion in conspiracy-theory thinking can erode religious faith rather than simply harming mental health, drawing on the experience of Utahn Kris Kofoed, who stepped back from alternative-media podcasts after feeling they were taking over his thinking. Pontifical University of the Holy Cross media dean Daniel Asara told Deseret News that believing powerful hidden actors control world events can create contradictions with core religious teachings, like trusting in God's providence. Hess notes that suspicion of "secret combinations" has deep roots in Latter-day Saint scripture, and cites Rutgers scholar Jack Z. Bratich and Boise State researchers on how the "conspiracy theorist" label itself can be misused to dismiss legitimate concerns. The piece argues that while seeking broader explanations for confusing events is natural, all-encompassing conspiratorial thinking can turn spirituality into something obsessive or defensive rather than a genuine motivating force.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Hess

item.title: More Salt Lake Temple open house tickets dropping in 2 upcoming waves
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced two more waves of ticket releases, on Sept. 15 and Oct. 1, for the public to tour the renovated Salt Lake Temple ahead of its 2027 open house. President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the Quorum of the Twelve told a press event inside the temple that leaders are "reaching out to all the world" to invite visitors, after the first 1 million tickets were claimed within 24 hours; church and civic leaders expect 4 to 5 million total visitors during the six-month celebration. The open house, themed "Rejoice in Christ," runs April 5 through Oct. 1, 2027, and will mark the first public access to the temple's interior in 134 years, featuring exhibits, performances and films. Tickets are available through TempleSquare.org or the Temple Square app, and a virtual tour option will be offered for those unable to travel to Salt Lake City.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Church News podcast: Hope in the modern dating landscape
item.description: In episode 311 of the Church News podcast, Brigham Young University marriage-preparation researcher Jason S. Carroll joins reporter Mary Richards to discuss findings from the National Dating Landscape Survey, a recent study showing only about one in three young U.S. adults are actively dating amid a broader decline in marriage and birth rates. Carroll, director of the Family Initiative at BYU's Wheatley Institute and a 20-year marriage-prep instructor, highlights "positive outlier" patterns from the research that he says point toward building a healthier dating and marriage culture. The episode is framed around teachings from Church President Dallin H. Oaks that family is central to Latter-day Saint doctrine, even as courtship trends shift nationally.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Embrace the awkward: It can create 'honor code-appropriate sparks,' BYU president tells students
item.description: BYU President Shane Reese urged students at the university's fall devotional to put down their phones and pursue in-person connection, telling them to "embrace the awkward" as a path to growth, dating and marriage. Reese cited data showing married BYU student rates have fallen to 17% from 25% in 2021, and shared stories of leaders who met their spouses by working up the courage to talk to someone waiting in line. He argued that friction and productive struggle, not frictionless scrolling through social media, build discernment, character and relationships, warning that letting artificial intelligence think or write for students won't develop their intellect or social skills. Reese framed Jesus Christ's outward focus on people like Zacchaeus as a model for turning attention away from screens.
